brief.text: India had an open-source epic thousands of years before open-source software, Amit Varma joked: no single Ramayana, but many retellings, each adapted to its region and its time. {069-C12}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why we retell stories
lead.head: Once upon the same time
body: Picture a prehistoric human with no clothes, no cellphone and no internet. A bright orange object rises and falls in the sky, day after day, and he has no idea what is going on. What does he do?
“You make up a story about it,” Amit Varma said, “and thus you have sun gods, and thus you have the beginning of religion.” {069-S01}
Storytelling, Varma argued, is the first human instinct. The world is deeply complex, every story simplifies it, and without stories we would be paralysed into inaction.
Ajay Shah agreed. Science and amusement are both stories, he said, on a spectrum of how fanciful and how connected to reality. “We are not robots, we’re not computers, we are not LLMs, we’re human.”
Then came the question behind the episode. We seem to tell an infinite number of stories. Why do we tell the ones we do?
## Only seven plots
Varma took his answer from a book he read many years back, Christopher Booker’s *The Seven Basic Plots*. Its claim is that there are only so many storylines, and we fit everything into them.

So *Beowulf* and the *Epic of Gilgamesh*, *Jaws* and the James Bond films, and *Sholay* are “all basically the same story”, Varma said. “They might seem completely different, but you’ve changed settings, you’ve changed characters.” {069-C02}

The seven are Overcoming the Monster, Rags to Riches, the Quest, Voyage and Return, Comedy, Tragedy and Rebirth. They blend into one another. *The Lord of the Rings* and the Mahabharata, Varma said, contain all seven.

Booker gives each its own five acts. Underneath, Varma said, the shape is constant: “You start in a quiet place and then shit happens and then you end in a quiet place.” The end can be death or happiness.
## A structure, not a cage
Varma was careful not to be prescriptive. Modern literature and cinema go beyond these plots, he told writers, and they should follow their hearts.
Formula is real enough. Sturgeon’s Law, he said, holds that 95 per cent of everything is crap, and studio executives try to force templates on filmmakers.

But the answer, Varma argued, is not to abandon form. “The way to break out of mediocrity is not to break out of the structure. It is to do interesting things within the structure and make it work for you.” {069-C04}
## Whose story is it?
Which plot a story follows can depend on whose eyes you see it through. Give Goliath a backstory, Varma said, and David and Goliath becomes a tragedy. {069-C09}
A live war is a plot whose genre is not yet settled. Shah cast the Battle of Kyiv as Overcoming the Monster; Varma warned that it could still end as tragedy.

Varma closed with a passage from Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s *The Gulag Archipelago*, which Booker quotes at the start of his chapter on rebirth. The line between good and evil, it says, runs through every human heart, and it moves over time. {069-C13}
Then it started raining. “We are not in a studio with green screen,” Varma said, and the hosts would have to rush back inside. First, though, he made a plea.
Stories have to simplify, he said, often into black and white. The real world is complicated. “Let us not rush to judgment. Let us not think we are good and others are evil.”
Within all of us, Varma said, are hero and villain, comedy and tragedy, David and Goliath. The stories he would love storytellers to tell are ones that embrace this complexity.

second.label: Overcoming the monster
second.head: Kyiv’s unfinished script
second.deck: Ajay Shah casts the Battle of Kyiv as Booker’s first plot
body: Life in Ukraine was normal until a monster invaded from the north, Ajay Shah said, recalling the Battle of Kyiv from the hosts’ episodes on stories that should be films. The world, Shah included, assumed Ukraine would fall. {069-S05}

Then the scrappy Ukrainians, armed with artillery and Javelin missiles, stopped the monster in his tracks. Amit Varma promised to buy Shah a kurta and a patiala “because there is an artist in you”. {069-J03}

Varma mapped it onto the monster plot’s five acts: the call, initial success, confrontation, final ordeal, miraculous escape. But this is the real world, he added. The ending is unwritten, and it could yet be a tragedy.

quote.text: It’s only a question of when Ukraine will be conquered, not whether, and myself included.

second.caption: the Battle of Kyiv

third.head: Scrooge on a slow train
body: Ajay Shah has seen few films, but he has seen *Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge*. What he remembers is the last scene: the slow train at an obscure station, a feeling anyone who has made such journeys knows. {#slowtrain}
Amit Varma used the film twice. First it served as voyage and return, a journey from which the travellers come back changed. Then he went back to its climax: “Ja Simran, jee le apni zindagi”.
What matters there, Varma said, is what happens to the stern father played by Amrish Puri. “He changes. He is reborn.” {069-S10}

Varma compared him to Scrooge in Dickens’ *A Christmas Carol*. Change happens in every plot, he said, but in a rebirth story it is the whole point: someone becomes a fundamentally different person. {069-C11}
third.caption: Amrish Puri’s rebirth

p2.title: The seven plots
p2.deck: Christopher Booker’s *The Seven Basic Plots*, plot by plot, as Amit Varma read it and Ajay Shah tested it. {069-R01}

sections.label: The prologue
sections.head: One arc, many costumes
sections.caption: how Booker found his pattern
body: Christopher Booker noticed the pattern while reading several works at once. {#simultaneous} Among them were *Macbeth* and *Lolita*, and he watched Truffaut’s film *Jules et Jim*. The same thing, Amit Varma said, was happening in all of them.

Each begins with a hero who is in some way unfulfilled, and a mood of anticipation. He finds a focus for his desires and enjoys dreamlike success: Macbeth becomes king, Humbert begins his affair with Lolita, Icarus discovers he can fly, Faust gets the devil’s magic.

“But gradually the mood of the story darkens,” Booker writes. {069-S02} The dream turns into a nightmare and ends in violent self-destruction. Varma said the same arc runs through *Romeo and Juliet* and *Madame Bovary*.
## Quiet, trouble, quiet
Anyone in Versova, Varma said, has no doubt tried writing screenplays, and knows Syd Field’s three-act structure: set-up, conflict, resolution. {069-J12}
Booker gives each archetype its own five acts. The acts differ, but the shape holds: a quiet start, an upheaval, a quiet end, whether in death or happiness. {069-C03}

~ Ajay Shah wondered whether each of the seven could become a thousand-word prompt for an LLM to mass-produce fiction. {#thousandword} A dreary use, he conceded, and not where Varma was. A lot of rubbish writing, he added, is already being done with LLMs.

quote.text: Finally, seemingly inexorably, the story works up to a climax of violent self-destruction. The dream ends in death.
quote.who: Christopher Booker, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The first plot
sections.head: Beowulf, meet the shark
sections.caption: overcoming the monster
body: The first archetype, Amit Varma announced, is overcoming the Indian state. He was kidding. It is overcoming the monster. {069-J01}
It runs from the *Epic of Gilgamesh* and *Beowulf* to the James Bond films, *Star Wars* and *Jaws*. Booker, Varma said, compares *Beowulf* with *Jaws* and finds them basically the same story.
In India there are *Sholay* and *Krrish*. The monster can be a human embodiment or a literal one, as in *Jurassic Park* or *King Kong*.
The arc is simple: things are normal, a monster arrives, things go badly, and eventually we win. Unless, Varma added, the monster is the Indian state, a film he does not think has been written yet.
## When we lose

Ajay Shah objected that if the story ends in defeat, it is not this type. Then it is tragedy, Varma replied. Story types merge, he said: *The Lord of the Rings* and Harry Potter both kill off a big monster, but carry other arcs too.
Booker’s five acts for this plot are the call, initial success, confrontation, final ordeal and miraculous escape, common, Varma said, to all the James Bond films. {#fiveacts}
~ Ukraine fits so far, Varma said: Zelensky in his office, something happens, then initial success. But this is the real world. It is story type one or story type five, Shah said. {#typefive}

quote.text: Unless that monster is a Indian state. I don’t think that film has been written yet.

sections.label: The third plot
sections.head: In search of number three
sections.caption: the quest
body: “Are you on a quest to find number three?” Amit Varma asked. “Number three is a quest.” {069-J05}

You search for something, go on a journey and eventually find it. It is in many ways the oldest archetype, Varma said: the *Odyssey*, *Pilgrim’s Progress* and *The Divine Comedy* centre on it, as do *Raiders of the Lost Ark*, *Finding Nemo* and *Chennai Express*.
Ajay Shah asked whether the Manhattan Project counted. Absolutely, said Varma, adding that the Oppenheimer story is also a tragedy. “I’m very good at identifying tragedy, you see.” {069-J06}

Shah’s pick was Tracy Kidder’s *The Soul of a New Machine*: a journalist embedded at Data General as a team builds one CPU. It takes you into the minds of the engineers and their leader, Tom West, and the emptiness after it is finished. {069-R02}
## Five stages
The acts are the call, the journey, arrival and frustration, the final ordeal and the goal.

~ Varma read Shah’s own life as a quest. After IIT and a PhD in economics in the US, Shah chose to come back to India, when kids of his generation saw getting out as escaping. The quest, to make India a better place, is ongoing. {069-S08}

quote.text: You made the call to come back, and the quest of course is make India a better place, and I guess that’s ongoing

sections.label: The fourth plot
sections.head: Gone to Goa, back changed
sections.caption: voyage and return
body: Ajay Shah complained that three plots in, there had not been enough romance. {#romance} So Amit Varma asked him what DDLJ stood for.

The fourth archetype is voyage and return: you make a journey, you come back, and usually you come back changed. *Alice in Wonderland*, *Peter Pan*, *The Time Machine* and *Back to the Future* fit, Varma said, as do DDLJ, *Dil Chahta Hai*, with its trip to Goa, *Jab We Met* and *Queen*.
Why does it appeal? Many people feel stuck, Varma said, living what Thoreau called lives of quiet desperation, and it is attractive to think that going somewhere will change them. {069-J15}
Shah recalled a line he attributed to Robert McNamara: we go on the journey, and when we come back we understand where we had been. {#mcnamara}
## Hobbit or ring?

The acts run from anticipation and initial fascination to frustration, nightmare, and escape and return. Varma’s idea of nightmare: a trek on which you break your leg and hang off a cliff, sure you will die.

~ Shah drew a fine line. *The Hobbit* belongs here, he said: they go out on a finite problem, to slay a dragon, and come back changed. {#hobbit} Then they are ready for the quest, *The Lord of the Rings*, which is structurally different.

quote.text: The zen you find at the top of the mountain is the zen that you take with yourself.

sections.label: The fifth plot
sections.head: No laugh track required
sections.caption: comedy as a structure
body: Comedy, in Christopher Booker’s sense, is not about making you laugh, Amit Varma said. It is a structure: a little world under a shadow of confusion, a nightmarish tangle, then a revelation that brings everyone together in joyful reunion. {#littleworld}

As a boy, Varma saw Shakespeare’s plays sorted into comedies and tragedies, and took comedy to mean whatever made him laugh. But the genre runs on misunderstandings, mistaken identities and confusion, all cleared up for a happy ending.

Booker lists four common elements. Characters imprisoned in anger, greed or jealousy must change, or be shown up. True identities are revealed. People find their other halves. Whatever was lost is restored.
## Love and laughter part ways

Ajay Shah doubted that the form survived in twentieth-century literature: “we don’t take P. G. Wodehouse as serious literature”. Wodehouse, Varma replied, is one of its finest examples, and Jane Austen’s *Pride and Prejudice*, *Sense and Sensibility* and *Emma* are comedies in structure. {069-J18}
In the twentieth century, Booker argues, love and laughter went their separate ways. A rom-com may not have much laughter, Varma said, and in *Housefull* romance is not central. {069-C07}

~ Every Mills and Boon book follows the structure, Varma said. {069-J08} How to refer to thirty of them in the plural, nobody could settle. Shah offered an easier one: the plural of Attorney General is Attorneys General.

quote.text: But now love and laughter have kind of gone in different directions.

sections.label: The sixth plot
sections.head: Goliath’s side of the story
sections.caption: tragedy and point of view
body: Tragedy, Amit Varma said, follows a noble protagonist lured into ignoble acts until everything falls apart, usually in death. The form runs from *Oedipus Rex* to *Macbeth*, *Hamlet* and *Julius Caesar*.

In *Julius Caesar*, he said, the tragedy is not Caesar’s but Brutus’s, a noble man who debases himself. {#brutus} Ajay Shah likened the opening stage of anticipation to the warning to beware the Ides of March.
*Bonnie and Clyde* and *Jules et Jim* fit, and in India *Devdas*, though of Sanjay Leela Bhansali’s version, Varma said, “the film itself was a tragedy”. {069-J10}
## Whose eyes?
The genre depends on point of view. Give Goliath a backstory, Varma said, trapped in his image of strength, never having found love, and David and Goliath becomes a tragedy. {069-C09}

In his writing course, he asks students to retell a known story from another point of view. Some have told *Sholay* from Gabbar Singh’s side, or Harry Potter from Voldemort’s, with backstories in which the villain is a victim of circumstance. {069-S11}

~ Shah suggested the Mahabharata from Draupadi’s point of view. Varma called the epic a masterpiece that survives as magnificent storytelling, not only through religion. One of his favourite books of all time, Irawati Karve’s *Yuganta*, is candid about its misogyny.

quote.text: Maybe Goliath sees the stone coming from the catapult and he chooses to let it hit him.

side.boxText: Christopher Booker’s *The Seven Basic Plots* argues that every story recycles one of seven archetypes. Amit Varma read it many years back, calls it excellent, and offers it as a lens for writers, not a rulebook. {069-R01}

contQuote.text: Gradually it became clear to me that the line separating good from evil runs not between states, not between classes, and not between parties. It runs through the heart of each and every one of us

stories.caption: Mukulika Banerjee’s quest
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on two quests told side by side
stories.head: A quest that kept her awake
body: In one of the hosts’ episodes on stories that should be films, Amit Varma told two stories at once, decades apart, and both were quests. {#twoquests} Here he used them to illustrate the third plot.
In one, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan sets out to defeat the British Empire, and then to make something of the new nation. He succeeds in the first quest, Varma said, and fails in the second.
In the other, Mukulika Banerjee goes to the Pathan areas of Pakistan to find survivors of the Khudai Khidmatgar.

Her question was why “a people who are supposed to be violent Pathans could take part in the greatest nonviolent movement of all time”, and lead it with original thinking. {069-S09} Varma urged listeners to read her book, *The Pathan Unarmed*.

Her call, in Booker’s terms, came from her PhD adviser, who told her to do a PhD only if something kept her awake at night. {#awake} Then came the journey, and the difficulty of finding surviving members.
The final ordeal, Varma said, belonged less to her than to Ghaffar Khan, whose freedom movement had its arc and its low moments. Then comes the goal, and the quest is over.

~ Ajay Shah had been well briefed. When Banerjee came to the XKDR Forum office a couple of months earlier, he said, “I smiled at her with an extra thousand words because of all the things you told me.” {#programmed}
stories.why: A quest can end in victory and heartbreak at once, as Ghaffar Khan’s did. And the call need not be grand: sometimes it is a single question about what keeps you awake at night.
stories.postscript: Varma also interviewed Banerjee for his podcast, *The Seen and the Unseen*, and told listeners to hear that episode too.

stories.caption: the CIA’s call to the climbers
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the call that opens every quest
stories.head: Nanda Devi, on the house
body: When Amit Varma described the call that opens a quest, Ajay Shah remembered a story from one of their episodes: a plutonium-powered device meant to be mounted on top of Nanda Devi, in a mission that went terribly wrong.

What stayed with him was one paragraph. Quietly, one by one, the CIA approached the world’s most elite climbers with an offer: climb Nanda Devi, all expenses paid. {069-S06} There was just one minor detail. “You’re gonna have to do some work for us.”

Shah’s own call was quieter. He was part of a project to climb Kokankada in the Sahyadris, and remembers vividly how its leader, Girish Sant, “took me aside one evening saying, Do you want to come on this?” {069-S07}
~ That, Shah said, is the great moment: come, let’s go do it.
stories.why: The call to adventure often arrives as an irresistible offer, with the catch in the small print. And in real life it is rarely dramatic: one person quietly asks another whether they are in.

stories.start: What is common to Sylvester Stralone, Julia Roberts, Anne Hathaway, and Ranweer Kapoor?
stories.end: we'll give you a lot of money. Fuck you I wanna act in it.
stories.caption: Stallone’s refusal
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the second plot, rags to riches
stories.head: Keep your money, I’m Rocky
body: Amit Varma opened the second archetype with a quiz: what do Sylvester Stallone, Julia Roberts, Anne Hathaway and Ranbir Kapoor have in common? {#quiz} Ajay Shah remembered a story Varma had told him: Stallone wrote *Rocky*.

He did, Varma said, and he wanted to act in it. The studio offered a lot of money for the script, as long as someone else played the part. Stallone’s reply, as Varma told it: “Fuck you I wanna act in it.” {069-S03}

*Rocky* is rags to riches, as are *Pretty Woman*, *The Devil Wears Prada* and *Rockstar*, and long before them *Cinderella* and *Aladdin*. Most people dream of being much better off, Varma said, so it is a trope everyone can identify with.
~ Varma did not count himself among them. “My life sadly only rags,” he said. {069-J04}
stories.why: By turning down the safe deal, Stallone made his own life a rags-to-riches story, the same plot as the film he would not give up. Varma called it quite brilliant.

stories.start: my father's story. Tell me about your father's story.
stories.end: your story, will it be tragedy? Are you gonna let him down?
stories.caption: his father’s story
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s father, and a tease about the sequel
stories.head: From Hyderabad, Sindh, to CMIE
body: Rags to riches is not only for the movies. Asked by Amit Varma for his father’s story, Ajay Shah said it began in Hyderabad, Sindh, in what is now Pakistan, where there was just nothing around.
From there, his father ended up as “one of the cool economists of the country” and founded CMIE, “all in a short fifty eight years”. {069-S04}
Varma called it a beautiful story, then turned to the son. “Your story, will it be tragedy? Are you gonna let him down?” {#letdown} “Riches to rags,” came the answer.
~ Asked late in the episode whether he had ever been reborn, Shah said not in fundamental ways. “Lots of implementation detail has happened, but the foundations were the same.” {069-J11}
stories.why: The archetype is not only for fairy tales: it describes real lives. And one family can hold more than one plot, as Varma’s tease to the son showed within moments.

quiz.q: Which film did Christopher Booker compare with Beowulf, finding them basically the same story?
quiz.a: *Jaws*. Both are tales of overcoming the monster, the first of the seven plots.

quiz.q: According to Sturgeon’s Law, as Amit Varma cited it, what share of everything is crap?
quiz.a: Ninety-five per cent, which is why so much formula writing is mediocre.

quiz.q: What did the studio want from Sylvester Stallone, and what did he insist on?
quiz.a: To buy his *Rocky* script; he insisted on acting in it himself.

quiz.q: In *Julius Caesar*, whose tragedy is it, according to Amit Varma?
quiz.a: Brutus’s, a noble man who debases himself and suffers for it.

quiz.q: Which DDLJ character does Varma say is truly reborn, and which Dickens figure does he resemble?
quiz.a: The father played by Amrish Puri, compared to Scrooge in *A Christmas Carol*.

quiz.q: What did Varma say India had, thousands of years before open-source software?
quiz.a: An open-source epic: the Ramayana, retold differently in every region and era.
